answer:
RESULTS: estimated coefficients, group-specific slopes, gamma tests, robustness table, and the final hypothesis.

==================== MAIN ESTIMATES ====================
Outcome log(GNI pc, constant 2015 US$) on lagged education expenditure (% of GNI), LMC dummy, interaction, N=10 (2011–2015 overlap, the only window where SSA income exists):
  beta_SSA = −0.111 (se 0.058 OLS / 0.013 HAC), beta_LMC = −0.728 (se 0.045 HAC)
  gamma (LMC interaction) = −0.617, Wald chi2 = 177.7, p < 0.001 → the negative income–expenditure association is significantly steeper in LMC than SSA in levels; the SSA slope is roughly 1/6–1/7 of the LMC slope magnitude.
  Adding the only df-affordable control (lagged secondary enrollment): beta_SSA = −0.044, beta_LMC = −0.362, gamma = −0.319 (Wald p < 0.001 HAC; p ≈ 0.08 by OLS t). Lagged enrollment itself enters positive (+0.010 per pp, p = 0.03).

==================== ROBUSTNESS TABLE ====================
Income equation, branch (a), 2011–2015 overlap (N=10):
  1. Levels, HAC(2):          beta_SSA −0.111 | beta_LMC −0.728 | gamma −0.617*** (Wald p<0.001)
  2. Levels + lag_sec, HAC:   beta_SSA −0.044 | beta_LMC −0.362 | gamma −0.319*** (p<0.001 HAC; p≈0.08 OLS)
  3. Levels, GLS AR(1):       beta_SSA −0.064 | beta_LMC −0.109 | gamma −0.045 (se 0.134, n.s.)
  4. First differences, HAC:  beta_SSA −0.051 | beta_LMC +0.002 | gamma +0.053 (p=0.19, n.s.)
LMC income equation, full window (1975–2015, log GNI pc on lagged edu exp + trend):
  bivariate+trend, HAC: −0.212*** (se 0.051, N=40) | same, GLS AR(1): +0.014 (se 0.015, n.s.)
  1991–2015 balanced + controls (lag_sec, lag_exp, lag_lfp) + trend: −0.106 (se 0.071, p=0.14, N=24)
  excluding crisis years 2008–2010: bivariate −0.208*** (p<0.001); with controls −0.156 (p=0.083)
  first differences: −0.026 (p=0.55)
Enrollment channel (branch b; lagged edu exp → enrollment, group-specific trends, LMC interaction):
  secondary 1975–2015: SSA −3.06 | LMC −3.29 | gamma −0.24 (p=0.88) — no group difference
  secondary 1991–2015: SSA −0.36 | LMC −0.94 | gamma −0.58 (p=0.82)
  primary 1975–2015:   SSA −5.18 | LMC −0.81 | gamma +4.37 (p=0.007) — but the 1991–2015 window flips the sign (gamma −6.31, p=0.38), so this single significant contrast is window-fragile
  Δ secondary (FD):    SSA −0.08 | LMC +0.13 | gamma +0.21 (p=0.57)

==================== INTERPRETATION ====================
Direction: contrary to the growth story the brief implies, higher lagged education-expenditure shares are associated with slightly LOWER per capita income in both groups in levels. This is a compositional artifact: in both groups the expenditure share drifted down (SSF 4.30→3.15, LMC ~3.7→3.06 % of GNI) while per capita income rose (LMC $840→$1965; SSA $1555→$1634 in 2011–2015), so any within-group correlation is dominated by opposing trends. Once serial correlation is absorbed (GLS AR(1)) or trends differenced out (FD), every income coefficient collapses to economic and statistical zero — LMC full-window even flips sign (+0.014, n.s.) under AR(1).
Comparison: the levels specifications consistently put the SSA slope flatter (less negative) than LMC — about 1/6 to 1/8 the magnitude (−0.11 vs −0.73; −0.04 vs −0.36) — and the raw 2011–2015 interaction is significant. But that significance does not survive AR(1) errors (gamma −0.045, se 0.134) or first differencing (gamma +0.053, p=0.19), and the enrollment-channel comparison (where SSA has full 1975–2015 data) shows no significant group difference in secondary enrollment (p=0.82–0.88) and an unstable one in primary. Also note the small-sample HAC SEs in the N=10 model are unreliable (HAC se 0.013 < OLS se 0.058 for beta_SSA), another reason not to lean on the raw interaction.
Verdict: the data do not support a robust claim that the effect differs between SSA and LMC; what they support is that in BOTH groups the income–education-expenditure association is near zero once trends/serial correlation are handled, with the point estimates consistently less negative for SSA than LMC.

==================== FINAL HYPOTHESIS (submission answer) ====================
"Across 1975–2015, rising per capita income (GNI per capita, constant 2015 US$) in both Sub-Saharan Africa and lower-middle-income countries coincided with a declining education-expenditure share of GNI, so that — measured associationally, with lagged expenditure, group trends and HAC/AR(1) errors — the estimated effect of education expenditure on per capita income is not positive in either group: in the 2011–2015 window where SSA income is observed, a 1 percentage-point-of-GNI higher lagged education share is associated with roughly 0.04–0.11 log points (~4–11%) lower per capita income in SSA versus roughly 0.36–0.73 log points (~36–73%) lower in LMC, i.e. the negative association is consistently flatter in SSA — approximately one-sixth to one-eighth the LMC magnitude — and the raw SSA-vs-LMC difference is nominally significant (Wald p<0.001) but does not survive AR(1) or first-difference specifications; therefore the defensible hypothesis is that the income association with education expenditure is similarly weak (effectively zero after accounting for trends) in both groups, with no detectable SSA–LMC difference in the education-spending–income relationship, and SSA's consistently flatter slope suggesting, at most, a smaller negative association rather than a distinct positive effect."

==================== WORKFLOW (accompanying description) ====================
Variable mapping (explicit): outcome = GNI per capita, constant 2015 US$ (NY.GNP.PCAP.KD) — the file contains GNI per capita constant 2015 US$, not the "per capita GDP 2010 US$" named in the brief; treatment = Adjusted savings: education expenditure (% of GNI) (NY.ADJ.AEDU.GN.ZS) — a savings-side aggregate, not the government-expenditure-share the brief describes; controls = secondary/primary gross enrollment, export growth, labor force participation. SSA coverage limitation: SSA income exists only for 2011–2015 (5 of 41 years; 88% missing), so the income-effect comparison rests on a 10-observation overlap window, while the full-window branch routes SSA through the enrollment channel (complete 1975–2015); SSA income was NOT imputed from LMC. Data are two group-level aggregate time series (SSF, LMC), not a country panel, so fixed effects degenerate to the group dummy; inference is associational only. Executed script: analysis_education_gdp.py (loads the CSV, tidies wide→long, runs branch (a), the LMC full-window models, the enrollment-channel branch (b), the four approved robustness checks, and the Wald tests).

Limitations: N=10 main window (4–5 obs/group), HAC small-sample unreliability, group aggregates only (no country-level variation), and "developing countries" proxied by the narrower LMC classification.

payload.workflow: Tidied the WB wide CSV (12 rows = 6 series × 2 groups, 41 year columns; empty cells = missing, no '..' markers) into a group-year panel. Outcome: GNI per capita constant 2015 US$ (NY.GNP.PCAP.KD; file supersedes the brief's 'per capita GDP 2010 US$'). Treatment: adjusted savings education expenditure, % of GNI (NY.ADJ.AEDU.GN.ZS). Controls: gross primary/secondary enrollment, export growth, labor force participation (1991–2015 coverage). Main model: log GNI pc on lagged (t−1) education expenditure, LMC dummy, LMC×expenditure interaction, group-specific trends, HAC(Newey-West)/GLS-AR(1) errors; gamma (interaction) is the SSA-vs-LMC comparison, tested by Wald. SSA income is observed only 2011–2015 (5/41 years), so the income comparison runs on the 2011–2015 overlap (N=10) and SSA is additionally routed through the enrollment channel over the full 1975–2015 window (SSA income not imputed). Robustness (exactly four checks): levels vs first differences; balanced 1991–2015 window; exclusion of crisis years 2008–2010; HAC vs AR(1) errors. All coefficients collapse toward zero and lose significance under AR(1)/FD; group difference significant only in raw levels. Caveats: group-level aggregates only (N=2 units), small-sample HAC unreliable at N=10, LMC is a narrow proxy for 'developing countries', associational not causal.
